<!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[az:Meoto İva]][[ca:Meoto Iwa]][[co:commons:Category:Meoto-iwa]][[cs:Meoto Iwa]][[de:Meoto-Iwa]][[el:Μεότο Ίουα]][[en:Meoto Iwa]][[es:Meoto Iwa]][[eu:Meoto Iwa]][[fr:Meoto iwa]][[ha:Meoto Iwa]][[id:Meoto Iwa]][[it:Meoto Iwa]][[ja:夫婦岩]][[pl:Meoto Iwa]][[pt:Meoto-Iwa]][[ru:Мэото Ива]][[th:เมโอโตะอิวะ]][[tr:Meoto Iwa]][[zh:夫婦岩]] <!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[az:Meoto İva]][[ca:Meoto Iwa]][[co:commons:Category:Meoto-iwa]][[cs:Meoto Iwa]][[de:Meoto-Iwa]][[el:Μεότο Ίουα]][[en:Meoto Iwa]][[es:Meoto Iwa]][[eu:Meoto Iwa]][[fr:Meoto iwa]][[ha:Meoto Iwa]][[id:Meoto Iwa]][[it:Meoto Iwa]][[ja:夫婦岩]][[pl:Meoto Iwa]][[pt:Meoto-Iwa]][[ru:Мэото Ива]][[th:เมโอโตะอิวะ]][[tr:Meoto Iwa]][[zh:夫婦岩]] <!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[az:Meoto İva]][[ca:Meoto Iwa]][[sn:commons:Category:Meoto-iwa]][[cs:Meoto Iwa]][[de:Meoto-Iwa]][[el:Μεότο Ίουα]][[en:Meoto Iwa]][[es:Meoto Iwa]][[eu:Meoto Iwa]][[fr:Meoto iwa]][[ha:Meoto Iwa]][[id:Meoto Iwa]][[it:Meoto Iwa]][[ja:夫婦岩]][[pl:Meoto Iwa]][[pt:Meoto-Iwa]][[ru:Мэото Ива]][[th:เมโอโตะอิวะ]][[tr:Meoto Iwa]][[zh:夫婦岩]] {{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[da:d:Q333875]] Wikidata name: Meoto Iwa [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 08:08, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} {{Short description|Type of sacred rocks in Shinto}} {{distinguish|Meoto Rocks}} {{more citations needed|date=April 2022}}{{Split|date=June 2022|Meoto Iwa (Ise)|Meoto Iwa Rocks|discuss=Talk:Meoto Iwa#Split proposal}}[[File:Meotoiwa.jpg|right|thumb|250x250px|Meoto Iwa, the wedded rocks, daytime]] [[File:Meoto_Iwa_at_dusk.jpg|right|thumb|Meoto Iwa, the wedded rocks, at dusk]] {{nihongo|'''Meoto Iwa'''|夫婦岩}}, or '''Married Couple Rocks''', are a kind of rock formation seen as religiously significant in [[Shinto]]. They are a subtype of [[Iwakura rock]].
According to [[Shinto]], the rocks represent the union of the creator ''[[kami]]'', [[Izanagi]] and {{ill|Izanami|en|Izanami|WD=Q682306|lt=Izanami}}. The rocks, therefore, celebrate the union in marriage of man and woman.
The most famous pair is the pair at [[Futami Okitama Shrine]] in [[:en:Futami-ura|Futami-ura]], two rocky [[:en:Stack (Geology)|stacks]] off the coast from {{ill|Ise, Mie|en|Ise, Mie|WD=Q328067|lt=Ise, Mie}}, {{ill|Japan|en|Japan|WD=Q17|lt=Japan}}. They are joined by a ''{{ill|Shimenawa|en|Shimenawa|WD=Q1887421|lt=Shimenawa}}'' (a heavy rope of rice straw) and are considered sacred by worshippers of the shrine. The shimenawa, composed of five separate strands which each weigh 40 kilograms,<ref>{{cite web |title=Meoto-iwa rocks (Mie Prefecture) - Let's travel around Japan! |url=http://www.travel-around-japan.com/k54-07-meoto-iwa.html |access-date=13 March 2021 |website=Let's travel around Japan}}</ref> must be replaced several times a year in a special ceremony. The larger rock, said to be male, has a small ''[[torii]]'' at its peak.[[File:Hiroshige,_Futamigaura_in_Ise_Province,_1858.jpg|thumb|Fuji 36 Views of Ise Futamikaura" by [[:en:Hiroshige Utagawa|Hiroshige Utagawa]].]]At dawn during the summer, the sun appears to rise between the two rocks. {{ill|Mount Fuji|en|Mount Fuji|WD=Q39231|lt=Mount Fuji}} is visible in the distance. At low tide, the rocks are not separated by water.
[[Futami Okitama Shrine|Okitama Shrine]] is dedicated to [[Sarutahiko Ōkami]] and imperial food goddess [[Ukanomitama]]. There are numerous statues of frogs around the shrine. The shrine and the two rocks are near the [[:en:Grand Shrine of Ise|Grand Shrine of Ise]], the most important location of [[Misogi|purification]] in Shinto.
== Outline == The couple rocks at [[Futami Okitama Shrine]] in {{ill|Mie Prefecture|en|Mie Prefecture|WD=Q128196|lt=Mie Prefecture}} {{ill|Ise, Mie|en|Ise, Mie|WD=Q328067|lt=Ise City}} have been known for a long time, as depicted by {{ill|Ukiyo-e artist|ja|浮世絵師|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ukiyo-e artist|1=ukiyo-e artist|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q33082999}} in the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period}}, and are generally used as a symbol and prayer for marital bliss and domestic safety, maritime security and great catch, and is said to be a symbol of [[Iwakura rock|Iwakura Shinko]] in [[Ko-Shintō|Kojindo]], which means a symbolic place or object in {{ill|Nature|en|Nature|WD=Q7860|lt=Nature}}, especially megaliths, {{ill|Rock (geology)|en|Rock (geology)|WD=Q8063|lt=rocks}}, and {{ill|Mountain|en|Mountain|WD=Q8502|lt=Mountain}}s, were considered [[Shintai]]s and believed to be places where [[Kami]]s resided. For this reason, {{ill|Shimenawa|en|Shimenawa|WD=Q1887421|lt=Shimenawa}}s and [[torii]]s were decorated as proof that a deity resided there (kanzumaru).
It is also an embodiment of the {{ill|Concept|en|Concept|WD=Q151885|lt=Concept}} of the two sides of the same coin that pervades ancient Shinto and current [[shinto]]s, such as the idea that this world consists of Utsushi-yo and Tokoyo, and the [[Seven Lucky Gods]] of {{ill|Ebisu (mythology)|en|Ebisu (mythology)|WD=Q1129330|lt=Ebisu}} and Daikoku, two of the [[Seven Lucky Gods]], are believed to be one, and the counting of {{ill|Chopsticks|en|Chopsticks|WD=Q81980|lt=Chopsticks}} and {{ill|footwear|en|footwear|WD=Q161928|lt=footwear}} as one set or one pair is also said to be unique to Japan.
In the [[Kojiki]], there are many [[:en:myths|myths]] about married couples, from {{ill|Izanami|en|Izanami|WD=Q682306|lt=Izanami}} and [[Izanagi]] to [[Sarutahiko Ōkami]] and [[Ame-no-Uzume]]. It is thought that these became {{ill|Dōsojin|en|Dōsojin|WD=Q269515|lt=Sai no Kami}} and {{ill|Dōsojin|en|Dōsojin|WD=Q269515|lt=Dosojin}}, and were connected with the belief in a rock formation. This is why {{ill|Kṣitigarbha|en|Kṣitigarbha|WD=Q604687|lt=Jizo}}s and Dōsojin are often depicted as a couple or as a pair of large and small rocks or stone statues. This kind of belief in married couples has spread throughout the world over time and has become familiar in the form of married couple's bowls, etc. At the same time, it is deeply related to the belief in child-rearing and child-bearing in the framework of {{ill|Family|en|Family|WD=Q8436|lt=Family}}, such as {{ill|Ie (Japanese family system)|en|Ie (Japanese family system)|WD=Q1149315|lt=householder}} and home. The '<nowiki/>'''Iwana'''' are deeply related to the belief in child-bearing, child-rearing, and the treasure of children.
These ideas of '''rock-building belief''', '''Omote-Taiwanai''' and '''matrimonial belief''' (also called matrimonial harmony, which is the basis of {{ill|Veneration of the dead|en|Veneration of the dead|WD=Q238199|lt=ancestral spirit belief}}) are combined to form the object of enshrinement at the couple's rock.
== Oshimenawa == An example of an '''oshimenawa''' is Tateishi in {{ill|Futami, Mie|en|Futami, Mie|WD=Q5510468|lt=Futami Town}}, Ise City, Mie Prefecture. The large {{ill|Shimenawa|en|Shimenawa|WD=Q1887421|lt=Shimenawa}} rope connecting Tateishi and Nejiriwa, known as "husband and wife rocks," is believed to be the torii (gateway) to the offshore Kohtama Shrine stone, and is reattached three times a year in December (before the New Year), May, and September.<ref>[http://www.jingukaikan.jp/sukeikai/imgs_mimosuso/41.pdf Special Feature: Shimenawa at Ise] Jingu Kaikan reverence association</ref> During the shimenawa-renawa-renawa-renawa-renawa-renawa-renawa-renawa ceremony, a woodcarving song is sung, and some people take pieces of the old rope home as a good-luck charm for marital bliss.<ref>[http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mX_b2p0j14U husband-and-wife-iwa-dai-shimenawa-renawa-renawa-renawa-renawa-shikiji] Youtube 2010/12/19</ref>
== Influence == American composer {{ill|Roger Reynolds|en|Roger Reynolds|WD=Q673278|lt=Roger Reynolds}} took reference to the form of Meoto Iwa in Futami, where he visited in 1966, while composing the first movement "''Futami ga Ura''" of his second symphony, "''Symphony [Myths]''" (1990). Divided into 3 sections, the first and the last with "densely stratified texture" represent Izanagi and Izanami rocks respectively, and the middle section represents the space in-between.<ref>{{cite thesis |type=PhD |last=Summar |first=Sarah Page |date=December 2012 |title=Fidget, Sway, and Swerve: Three Works Inspired by Movement from the Intricate Maneuvers Series |publisher=University of North Texas |url=https://digital.library.unt.edu/ark%3A/67531/metadc177259/m2/1/high_res_d/dissertation.pdf}}</ref>
== National Married Couple Rocks Summit == The '''National Married Couple Rocks Summit Liaison Council''' has been formed by 10 tourist spots in Japan that have married couple rocks or rocks for married couples, and is holding the National Married Couple Rocks Summit.

{{Short description|Type of sacred rocks in Shinto}} {{distinguish|Meoto Rocks}} {{more citations needed|date=April 2022}}{{Split|date=June 2022|Meoto Iwa (Ise)|Meoto Iwa Rocks|discuss=Talk:Meoto Iwa#Split proposal}}[[File:Meotoiwa.jpg|right|thumb|250x250px|Meoto Iwa, the wedded rocks, daytime]] [[File:Meoto_Iwa_at_dusk.jpg|right|thumb|Meoto Iwa, the wedded rocks, at dusk]] {{nihongo|'''Meoto Iwa'''|夫婦岩}}, or '''Married Couple Rocks''', are a kind of rock formation seen as religiously significant in [[Shinto]]. They are a subtype of [[Iwakura rock]].
According to [[Shinto]], the rocks represent the union of the creator ''[[kami]]'', [[Izanagi]] and {{ill|Izanami|en|Izanami|WD=Q682306|lt=Izanami}}. The rocks, therefore, celebrate the union in marriage of man and woman.
The most famous pair is the pair at [[Futami Okitama Shrine]] in [[:en:Futami-ura|Futami-ura]], two rocky [[:en:Stack (Geology)|stacks]] off the coast from {{ill|Ise, Mie|en|Ise, Mie|WD=Q328067|lt=Ise, Mie}}, {{ill|Japan|en|Japan|WD=Q17|lt=Japan}}. They are joined by a ''{{ill|Shimenawa|en|Shimenawa|WD=Q1887421|lt=Shimenawa}}'' (a heavy rope of rice straw) and are considered sacred by worshippers of the shrine. The shimenawa, composed of five separate strands which each weigh 40 kilograms,<ref>{{cite web |title=Meoto-iwa rocks (Mie Prefecture) - Let's travel around Japan! |url=http://www.travel-around-japan.com/k54-07-meoto-iwa.html |access-date=13 March 2021 |website=Let's travel around Japan}}</ref> must be replaced several times a year in a special ceremony. The larger rock, said to be male, has a small ''[[torii]]'' at its peak.[[File:Hiroshige,_Futamigaura_in_Ise_Province,_1858.jpg|thumb|Fuji 36 Views of Ise Futamikaura" by [[:en:Hiroshige Utagawa|Hiroshige Utagawa]].]]At dawn during the summer, the sun appears to rise between the two rocks. {{ill|Mount Fuji|en|Mount Fuji|WD=Q39231|lt=Mount Fuji}} is visible in the distance. At low tide, the rocks are not separated by water.
[[Futami Okitama Shrine|Okitama Shrine]] is dedicated to [[Sarutahiko Ōkami]] and imperial food goddess [[Ukanomitama]]. There are numerous statues of frogs around the shrine. The shrine and the two rocks are near the [[:en:Grand Shrine of Ise|Grand Shrine of Ise]], the most important location of [[Misogi|purification]] in Shinto.
== Outline == The couple rocks at [[Futami Okitama Shrine]] in {{ill|Mie Prefecture|en|Mie Prefecture|WD=Q128196|lt=Mie Prefecture}} {{ill|Ise, Mie|en|Ise, Mie|WD=Q328067|lt=Ise City}} have been known for a long time, as depicted by {{ill|Ukiyo-e artist|ja|浮世絵師|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ukiyo-e artist|1=ukiyo-e artist|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q33082999}} in the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period}}, and are generally used as a symbol and prayer for marital bliss and domestic safety, maritime security and great catch, and is said to be a symbol of [[Iwakura rock|Iwakura Shinko]] in [[Ko-Shintō|Kojindo]], which means a symbolic place or object in {{ill|Nature|en|Nature|WD=Q7860|lt=Nature}}, especially megaliths, {{ill|Rock (geology)|en|Rock (geology)|WD=Q8063|lt=rocks}}, and {{ill|Mountain|en|Mountain|WD=Q8502|lt=Mountain}}s, were considered [[Shintai]]s and believed to be places where [[Kami]]s resided. For this reason, {{ill|Shimenawa|en|Shimenawa|WD=Q1887421|lt=Shimenawa}}s and [[torii]]s were decorated as proof that a deity resided there (kanzumaru).
It is also an embodiment of the {{ill|Concept|en|Concept|WD=Q151885|lt=Concept}} of the two sides of the same coin that pervades ancient Shinto and current [[shinto]]s, such as the idea that this world consists of Utsushi-yo and Tokoyo, and the [[Seven Lucky Gods]] of {{ill|Ebisu (mythology)|en|Ebisu (mythology)|WD=Q1129330|lt=Ebisu}} and Daikoku, two of the [[Seven Lucky Gods]], are believed to be one, and the counting of {{ill|Chopsticks|en|Chopsticks|WD=Q81980|lt=Chopsticks}} and {{ill|footwear|en|footwear|WD=Q161928|lt=footwear}} as one set or one pair is also said to be unique to Japan.
In the [[Kojiki]], there are many [[:en:myths|myths]] about married couples, from {{ill|Izanami|en|Izanami|WD=Q682306|lt=Izanami}} and [[Izanagi]] to [[Sarutahiko Ōkami]] and [[Ame-no-Uzume]]. It is thought that these became {{ill|Dōsojin|en|Dōsojin|WD=Q269515|lt=Sai no Kami}} and {{ill|Dōsojin|en|Dōsojin|WD=Q269515|lt=Dosojin}}, and were connected with the belief in a rock formation. This is why {{ill|Kṣitigarbha|en|Kṣitigarbha|WD=Q604687|lt=Jizo}}s and Dōsojin are often depicted as a couple or as a pair of large and small rocks or stone statues. This kind of belief in married couples has spread throughout the world over time and has become familiar in the form of married couple's bowls, etc. At the same time, it is deeply related to the belief in child-rearing and child-bearing in the framework of {{ill|Family|en|Family|WD=Q8436|lt=Family}}, such as {{ill|Ie (Japanese family system)|en|Ie (Japanese family system)|WD=Q1149315|lt=householder}} and home. The '<nowiki/>'''Iwana'''' are deeply related to the belief in child-bearing, child-rearing, and the treasure of children.
These ideas of '''rock-building belief''', '''Omote-Taiwanai''' and '''matrimonial belief''' (also called matrimonial harmony, which is the basis of {{ill|Veneration of the dead|en|Veneration of the dead|WD=Q238199|lt=ancestral spirit belief}}) are combined to form the object of enshrinement at the couple's rock.
== Oshimenawa == An example of an '''oshimenawa''' is Tateishi in {{ill|Futami, Mie|en|Futami, Mie|WD=Q5510468|lt=Futami Town}}, Ise City, Mie Prefecture. The large {{ill|Shimenawa|en|Shimenawa|WD=Q1887421|lt=Shimenawa}} rope connecting Tateishi and Nejiriwa, known as "husband and wife rocks," is believed to be the torii (gateway) to the offshore Kohtama Shrine stone, and is reattached three times a year in December (before the New Year), May, and September.<ref>[http://www.jingukaikan.jp/sukeikai/imgs_mimosuso/41.pdf Special Feature: Shimenawa at Ise] Jingu Kaikan reverence association</ref> During the shimenawa-renawa-renawa-renawa-renawa-renawa-renawa-renawa ceremony, a woodcarving song is sung, and some people take pieces of the old rope home as a good-luck charm for marital bliss.<ref>[http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mX_b2p0j14U husband-and-wife-iwa-dai-shimenawa-renawa-renawa-renawa-renawa-shikiji] Youtube 2010/12/19</ref>
== Influence == American composer {{ill|Roger Reynolds|en|Roger Reynolds|WD=Q673278|lt=Roger Reynolds}} took reference to the form of Meoto Iwa in Futami, where he visited in 1966, while composing the first movement "''Futami ga Ura''" of his second symphony, "''Symphony [Myths]''" (1990). Divided into 3 sections, the first and the last with "densely stratified texture" represent Izanagi and Izanami rocks respectively, and the middle section represents the space in-between.<ref>{{cite thesis |type=PhD |last=Summar |first=Sarah Page |date=December 2012 |title=Fidget, Sway, and Swerve: Three Works Inspired by Movement from the Intricate Maneuvers Series |publisher=University of North Texas |url=https://digital.library.unt.edu/ark%3A/67531/metadc177259/m2/1/high_res_d/dissertation.pdf}}</ref>
== National Married Couple Rocks Summit == The '''National Married Couple Rocks Summit Liaison Council''' has been formed by 10 tourist spots in Japan that have married couple rocks or rocks for married couples, and is holding the National Married Couple Rocks Summit.

{{Short description|Type of sacred rocks in Shinto}} {{distinguish|Meoto Rocks}} {{more citations needed|date=April 2022}}{{Split|date=June 2022|Meoto Iwa (Ise)|Meoto Iwa Rocks|discuss=Talk:Meoto Iwa#Split proposal}}[[File:Meotoiwa.jpg|right|thumb|250x250px|Meoto Iwa, the wedded rocks, daytime]] [[File:Meoto_Iwa_at_dusk.jpg|right|thumb|Meoto Iwa, the wedded rocks, at dusk]] {{nihongo|'''Meoto Iwa'''|夫婦岩}}, or '''Married Couple Rocks''', are a kind of rock formation seen as religiously significant in [[Shinto]]. They are a subtype of [[Iwakura rock]].
According to [[Shinto]], the rocks represent the union of the creator ''[[kami]]'', [[Izanagi]] and {{ill|Izanami|en|Izanami|WD=Q682306|lt=Izanami}}. The rocks, therefore, celebrate the union in marriage of man and woman.
The most famous pair is the pair at [[Futami Okitama Shrine]] in [[:en:Futami-ura|Futami-ura]], two rocky [[:en:Stack (Geology)|stacks]] off the coast from {{ill|Ise, Mie|en|Ise, Mie|WD=Q328067|lt=Ise, Mie}}, {{ill|Japan|en|Japan|WD=Q17|lt=Japan}}. They are joined by a ''{{ill|Shimenawa|en|Shimenawa|WD=Q1887421|lt=Shimenawa}}'' (a heavy rope of rice straw) and are considered sacred by worshippers of the shrine. The shimenawa, composed of five separate strands which each weigh 40 kilograms,<ref>{{cite web |title=Meoto-iwa rocks (Mie Prefecture) - Let's travel around Japan! |url=http://www.travel-around-japan.com/k54-07-meoto-iwa.html |access-date=13 March 2021 |website=Let's travel around Japan}}</ref> must be replaced several times a year in a special ceremony. The larger rock, said to be male, has a small ''[[torii]]'' at its peak.[[File:Hiroshige,_Futamigaura_in_Ise_Province,_1858.jpg|thumb|Fuji 36 Views of Ise Futamikaura" by [[:en:Hiroshige Utagawa|Hiroshige Utagawa]].]]At dawn during the summer, the sun appears to rise between the two rocks. {{ill|Mount Fuji|en|Mount Fuji|WD=Q39231|lt=Mount Fuji}} is visible in the distance. At low tide, the rocks are not separated by water.
[[Futami Okitama Shrine|Okitama Shrine]] is dedicated to [[Sarutahiko Ōkami]] and imperial food goddess [[Ukanomitama]]. There are numerous statues of frogs around the shrine. The shrine and the two rocks are near the [[:en:Grand Shrine of Ise|Grand Shrine of Ise]], the most important location of [[Misogi|purification]] in Shinto.
== Outline == The couple rocks at [[Futami Okitama Shrine]] in {{ill|Mie Prefecture|en|Mie Prefecture|WD=Q128196|lt=Mie Prefecture}} {{ill|Ise, Mie|en|Ise, Mie|WD=Q328067|lt=Ise City}} have been known for a long time, as depicted by {{ill|Ukiyo-e artist|ja|浮世絵師|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ukiyo-e artist|1=ukiyo-e artist|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q33082999}} in the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period}}, and are generally used as a symbol and prayer for marital bliss and domestic safety, maritime security and great catch, and is said to be a symbol of [[Iwakura rock|Iwakura Shinko]] in [[Ko-Shintō|Kojindo]], which means a symbolic place or object in {{ill|Nature|en|Nature|WD=Q7860|lt=Nature}}, especially megaliths, {{ill|Rock (geology)|en|Rock (geology)|WD=Q8063|lt=rocks}}, and {{ill|Mountain|en|Mountain|WD=Q8502|lt=Mountain}}s, were considered [[Shintai]]s and believed to be places where [[Kami]]s resided. For this reason, {{ill|Shimenawa|en|Shimenawa|WD=Q1887421|lt=Shimenawa}}s and [[torii]]s were decorated as proof that a deity resided there (kanzumaru).
It is also an embodiment of the {{ill|Concept|en|Concept|WD=Q151885|lt=Concept}} of the two sides of the same coin that pervades ancient Shinto and current [[shinto]]s, such as the idea that this world consists of Utsushi-yo and Tokoyo, and the [[Seven Lucky Gods]] of {{ill|Ebisu (mythology)|en|Ebisu (mythology)|WD=Q1129330|lt=Ebisu}} and Daikoku, two of the [[Seven Lucky Gods]], are believed to be one, and the counting of {{ill|Chopsticks|en|Chopsticks|WD=Q81980|lt=Chopsticks}} and {{ill|footwear|en|footwear|WD=Q161928|lt=footwear}} as one set or one pair is also said to be unique to Japan.
In the [[Kojiki]], there are many [[:en:myths|myths]] about married couples, from {{ill|Izanami|en|Izanami|WD=Q682306|lt=Izanami}} and [[Izanagi]] to [[Sarutahiko Ōkami]] and [[Ame-no-Uzume]]. It is thought that these became {{ill|Dōsojin|en|Dōsojin|WD=Q269515|lt=Sai no Kami}} and {{ill|Dōsojin|en|Dōsojin|WD=Q269515|lt=Dosojin}}, and were connected with the belief in a rock formation. This is why {{ill|Kṣitigarbha|en|Kṣitigarbha|WD=Q604687|lt=Jizo}}s and Dōsojin are often depicted as a couple or as a pair of large and small rocks or stone statues. This kind of belief in married couples has spread throughout the world over time and has become familiar in the form of married couple's bowls, etc. At the same time, it is deeply related to the belief in child-rearing and child-bearing in the framework of {{ill|Family|en|Family|WD=Q8436|lt=Family}}, such as {{ill|Ie (Japanese family system)|en|Ie (Japanese family system)|WD=Q1149315|lt=householder}} and home. The '<nowiki/>'''Iwana'''' are deeply related to the belief in child-bearing, child-rearing, and the treasure of children.
These ideas of '''rock-building belief''', '''Omote-Taiwanai''' and '''matrimonial belief''' (also called matrimonial harmony, which is the basis of {{ill|Veneration of the dead|en|Veneration of the dead|WD=Q238199|lt=ancestral spirit belief}}) are combined to form the object of enshrinement at the couple's rock.
== Oshimenawa == An example of an '''oshimenawa''' is Tateishi in {{ill|Futami, Mie|en|Futami, Mie|WD=Q5510468|lt=Futami Town}}, Ise City, Mie Prefecture. The large {{ill|Shimenawa|en|Shimenawa|WD=Q1887421|lt=Shimenawa}} rope connecting Tateishi and Nejiriwa, known as "husband and wife rocks," is believed to be the torii (gateway) to the offshore Kohtama Shrine stone, and is reattached three times a year in December (before the New Year), May, and September.<ref>[http://www.jingukaikan.jp/sukeikai/imgs_mimosuso/41.pdf Special Feature: Shimenawa at Ise] Jingu Kaikan reverence association</ref> During the shimenawa-renawa-renawa-renawa-renawa-renawa-renawa-renawa ceremony, a woodcarving song is sung, and some people take pieces of the old rope home as a good-luck charm for marital bliss.<ref>[http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mX_b2p0j14U husband-and-wife-iwa-dai-shimenawa-renawa-renawa-renawa-renawa-shikiji] Youtube 2010/12/19</ref>
== Influence == American composer {{ill|Roger Reynolds|en|Roger Reynolds|WD=Q673278|lt=Roger Reynolds}} took reference to the form of Meoto Iwa in Futami, where he visited in 1966, while composing the first movement "''Futami ga Ura''" of his second symphony, "''Symphony [Myths]''" (1990). Divided into 3 sections, the first and the last with "densely stratified texture" represent Izanagi and Izanami rocks respectively, and the middle section represents the space in-between.<ref>{{cite thesis |type=PhD |last=Summar |first=Sarah Page |date=December 2012 |title=Fidget, Sway, and Swerve: Three Works Inspired by Movement from the Intricate Maneuvers Series |publisher=University of North Texas |url=https://digital.library.unt.edu/ark%3A/67531/metadc177259/m2/1/high_res_d/dissertation.pdf}}</ref>
== National Married Couple Rocks Summit == The '''National Married Couple Rocks Summit Liaison Council''' has been formed by 10 tourist spots in Japan that have married couple rocks or rocks for married couples, and is holding the National Married Couple Rocks Summit.

{{Short description|Type of sacred rocks in Shinto}} {{distinguish|Meoto Rocks}} {{more citations needed|date=April 2022}}{{Split|date=June 2022|Meoto Iwa (Ise)|Meoto Iwa Rocks|discuss=Talk:Meoto Iwa#Split proposal}}[[File:Meotoiwa.jpg|right|thumb|250x250px|Meoto Iwa, the wedded rocks, daytime]] [[File:Meoto_Iwa_at_dusk.jpg|right|thumb|Meoto Iwa, the wedded rocks, at dusk]] {{nihongo|'''Meoto Iwa'''|夫婦岩}}, or '''Married Couple Rocks''', are a kind of rock formation seen as religiously significant in [[Shinto]]. They are a subtype of [[Iwakura rock]].
According to [[Shinto]], the rocks represent the union of the creator ''[[kami]]'', [[Izanagi]] and {{ill|Izanami|en|Izanami|WD=Q682306|lt=Izanami}}. The rocks, therefore, celebrate the union in marriage of man and woman.
The most famous pair is the pair at [[Futami Okitama Shrine]] in [[:en:Futami-ura|Futami-ura]], two rocky [[:en:Stack (Geology)|stacks]] off the coast from {{ill|Ise, Mie|en|Ise, Mie|WD=Q328067|lt=Ise, Mie}}, {{ill|Japan|en|Japan|WD=Q17|lt=Japan}}. They are joined by a ''{{ill|Shimenawa|en|Shimenawa|WD=Q1887421|lt=Shimenawa}}'' (a heavy rope of rice straw) and are considered sacred by worshippers of the shrine. The shimenawa, composed of five separate strands which each weigh 40 kilograms,<ref>{{cite web |title=Meoto-iwa rocks (Mie Prefecture) - Let's travel around Japan! |url=http://www.travel-around-japan.com/k54-07-meoto-iwa.html |access-date=13 March 2021 |website=Let's travel around Japan}}</ref> must be replaced several times a year in a special ceremony. The larger rock, said to be male, has a small ''[[torii]]'' at its peak.[[File:Hiroshige,_Futamigaura_in_Ise_Province,_1858.jpg|thumb|Fuji 36 Views of Ise Futamikaura" by [[:en:Hiroshige Utagawa|Hiroshige Utagawa]].]]At dawn during the summer, the sun appears to rise between the two rocks. {{ill|Mount Fuji|en|Mount Fuji|WD=Q39231|lt=Mount Fuji}} is visible in the distance. At low tide, the rocks are not separated by water.
[[Futami Okitama Shrine|Okitama Shrine]] is dedicated to [[Sarutahiko Ōkami]] and imperial food goddess [[Ukanomitama]]. There are numerous statues of frogs around the shrine. The shrine and the two rocks are near the [[:en:Grand Shrine of Ise|Grand Shrine of Ise]], the most important location of [[Misogi|purification]] in Shinto.
== Outline == The couple rocks at [[Futami Okitama Shrine]] in {{ill|Mie Prefecture|en|Mie Prefecture|WD=Q128196|lt=Mie Prefecture}} {{ill|Ise, Mie|en|Ise, Mie|WD=Q328067|lt=Ise City}} have been known for a long time, as depicted by {{ill|Ukiyo-e artist|ja|浮世絵師|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ukiyo-e artist|1=ukiyo-e artist|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q33082999}} in the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period}}, and are generally used as a symbol and prayer for marital bliss and domestic safety, maritime security and great catch, and is said to be a symbol of [[Iwakura rock|Iwakura Shinko]] in [[Ko-Shintō|Kojindo]], which means a symbolic place or object in {{ill|Nature|en|Nature|WD=Q7860|lt=Nature}}, especially megaliths, {{ill|Rock (geology)|en|Rock (geology)|WD=Q8063|lt=rocks}}, and {{ill|Mountain|en|Mountain|WD=Q8502|lt=Mountain}}s, were considered [[Shintai]]s and believed to be places where [[Kami]]s resided. For this reason, {{ill|Shimenawa|en|Shimenawa|WD=Q1887421|lt=Shimenawa}}s and [[torii]]s were decorated as proof that a deity resided there (kanzumaru).
It is also an embodiment of the {{ill|Concept|en|Concept|WD=Q151885|lt=Concept}} of the two sides of the same coin that pervades ancient Shinto and current [[shinto]]s, such as the idea that this world consists of Utsushi-yo and Tokoyo, and the [[Seven Lucky Gods]] of {{ill|Ebisu (mythology)|en|Ebisu (mythology)|WD=Q1129330|lt=Ebisu}} and Daikoku, two of the [[Seven Lucky Gods]], are believed to be one, and the counting of {{ill|Chopsticks|en|Chopsticks|WD=Q81980|lt=Chopsticks}} and {{ill|footwear|en|footwear|WD=Q161928|lt=footwear}} as one set or one pair is also said to be unique to Japan.
In the [[Kojiki]], there are many [[:en:myths|myths]] about married couples, from {{ill|Izanami|en|Izanami|WD=Q682306|lt=Izanami}} and [[Izanagi]] to [[Sarutahiko Ōkami]] and [[Ame-no-Uzume]]. It is thought that these became {{ill|Dōsojin|en|Dōsojin|WD=Q269515|lt=Sai no Kami}} and {{ill|Dōsojin|en|Dōsojin|WD=Q269515|lt=Dosojin}}, and were connected with the belief in a rock formation. This is why {{ill|Kṣitigarbha|en|Kṣitigarbha|WD=Q604687|lt=Jizo}}s and Dōsojin are often depicted as a couple or as a pair of large and small rocks or stone statues. This kind of belief in married couples has spread throughout the world over time and has become familiar in the form of married couple's bowls, etc. At the same time, it is deeply related to the belief in child-rearing and child-bearing in the framework of {{ill|Family|en|Family|WD=Q8436|lt=Family}}, such as {{ill|Ie (Japanese family system)|en|Ie (Japanese family system)|WD=Q1149315|lt=householder}} and home. The '<nowiki/>'''Iwana'''' are deeply related to the belief in child-bearing, child-rearing, and the treasure of children.
These ideas of '''rock-building belief''', '''Omote-Taiwanai''' and '''matrimonial belief''' (also called matrimonial harmony, which is the basis of {{ill|Veneration of the dead|en|Veneration of the dead|WD=Q238199|lt=ancestral spirit belief}}) are combined to form the object of enshrinement at the couple's rock.
== Oshimenawa == An example of an '''oshimenawa''' is Tateishi in {{ill|Futami, Mie|en|Futami, Mie|WD=Q5510468|lt=Futami Town}}, Ise City, Mie Prefecture. The large {{ill|Shimenawa|en|Shimenawa|WD=Q1887421|lt=Shimenawa}} rope connecting Tateishi and Nejiriwa, known as "husband and wife rocks," is believed to be the torii (gateway) to the offshore Kohtama Shrine stone, and is reattached three times a year in December (before the New Year), May, and September.<ref>[http://www.jingukaikan.jp/sukeikai/imgs_mimosuso/41.pdf Special Feature: Shimenawa at Ise] Jingu Kaikan reverence association</ref> During the shimenawa-renawa-renawa-renawa-renawa-renawa-renawa-renawa ceremony, a woodcarving song is sung, and some people take pieces of the old rope home as a good-luck charm for marital bliss.<ref>[http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mX_b2p0j14U husband-and-wife-iwa-dai-shimenawa-renawa-renawa-renawa-renawa-shikiji] Youtube 2010/12/19</ref>
== Influence == American composer {{ill|Roger Reynolds|en|Roger Reynolds|WD=Q673278|lt=Roger Reynolds}} took reference to the form of Meoto Iwa in Futami, where he visited in 1966, while composing the first movement "''Futami ga Ura''" of his second symphony, "''Symphony [Myths]''" (1990). Divided into 3 sections, the first and the last with "densely stratified texture" represent Izanagi and Izanami rocks respectively, and the middle section represents the space in-between.<ref>{{cite thesis |type=PhD |last=Summar |first=Sarah Page |date=December 2012 |title=Fidget, Sway, and Swerve: Three Works Inspired by Movement from the Intricate Maneuvers Series |publisher=University of North Texas |url=https://digital.library.unt.edu/ark%3A/67531/metadc177259/m2/1/high_res_d/dissertation.pdf}}</ref>
== National Married Couple Rocks Summit == The '''National Married Couple Rocks Summit Liaison Council''' has been formed by 10 tourist spots in Japan that have married couple rocks or rocks for married couples, and is holding the National Married Couple Rocks Summit.

{{Short description|Type of sacred rocks in Shinto}} {{distinguish|Meoto Rocks}} {{more citations needed|date=April 2022}}{{Split|date=June 2022|Meoto Iwa (Ise)|Meoto Iwa Rocks|discuss=Talk:Meoto Iwa#Split proposal}}[[File:Meotoiwa.jpg|right|thumb|250x250px|Meoto Iwa, the wedded rocks, daytime]] [[File:Meoto_Iwa_at_dusk.jpg|right|thumb|Meoto Iwa, the wedded rocks, at dusk]] {{nihongo|'''Meoto Iwa'''|夫婦岩}}, or '''Married Couple Rocks''', are a kind of rock formation seen as religiously significant in [[Shinto]]. They are a subtype of [[Iwakura rock]].
According to [[Shinto]], the rocks represent the union of the creator ''[[kami]]'', [[Izanagi]] and {{ill|Izanami|en|Izanami|WD=Q682306|lt=Izanami|1=Izanami}}. The rocks, therefore, celebrate the union in marriage of man and woman.
The most famous pair is the pair at [[Futami Okitama Shrine]] in [[:en:Futami-ura|Futami-ura]], two rocky [[:en:Stack (Geology)|stacks]] off the coast from {{ill|Ise, Mie|en|Ise, Mie|WD=Q328067|lt=Ise, Mie|1=Ise, Mie}}, {{ill|Japan|en|Japan|WD=Q17|lt=Japan|1=Japan}}. They are joined by a ''{{ill|Shimenawa|en|Shimenawa|WD=Q1887421|lt=Shimenawa|1=Shimenawa}}'' (a heavy rope of rice straw) and are considered sacred by worshippers of the shrine. The shimenawa, composed of five separate strands which each weigh 40 kilograms,<ref>{{cite web |title=Meoto-iwa rocks (Mie Prefecture) - Let's travel around Japan! |url=http://www.travel-around-japan.com/k54-07-meoto-iwa.html |access-date=13 March 2021 |website=Let's travel around Japan}}</ref> must be replaced several times a year in a special ceremony. The larger rock, said to be male, has a small ''[[torii]]'' at its peak.[[File:Hiroshige,_Futamigaura_in_Ise_Province,_1858.jpg|thumb|Fuji 36 Views of Ise Futamikaura" by [[:en:Hiroshige Utagawa|Hiroshige Utagawa]].]]At dawn during the summer, the sun appears to rise between the two rocks. {{ill|Mount Fuji|en|Mount Fuji|WD=Q39231|lt=Mount Fuji|1=Mount Fuji}} is visible in the distance. At low tide, the rocks are not separated by water.
[[Futami Okitama Shrine|Okitama Shrine]] is dedicated to [[Sarutahiko Ōkami]] and imperial food goddess [[Ukanomitama]]. There are numerous statues of frogs around the shrine. The shrine and the two rocks are near the [[:en:Grand Shrine of Ise|Grand Shrine of Ise]], the most important location of [[Misogi|purification]] in Shinto.
== Outline == The couple rocks at [[Futami Okitama Shrine]] in {{ill|Mie Prefecture|en|Mie Prefecture|WD=Q128196|lt=Mie Prefecture|1=Mie Prefecture}} {{ill|Ise, Mie|en|Ise, Mie|WD=Q328067|lt=Ise City|1=Ise, Mie}} have been known for a long time, as depicted by {{ill|Ukiyo-e artist|ja|浮世絵師|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ukiyo-e artist|1=ukiyo-e artist|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q33082999}} in the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period|1=Edo period}}, and are generally used as a symbol and prayer for marital bliss and domestic safety, maritime security and great catch, and is said to be a symbol of [[Iwakura rock|Iwakura Shinko]] in [[Ko-Shintō|Kojindo]], which means a symbolic place or object in {{ill|Nature|en|Nature|WD=Q7860|lt=Nature|1=Nature}}, especially megaliths, {{ill|Rock (geology)|en|Rock (geology)|WD=Q8063|lt=rocks|1=Rock (geology)}}, and {{ill|Mountain|en|Mountain|WD=Q8502|lt=Mountain|1=Mountain}}s, were considered [[Shintai]]s and believed to be places where [[Kami]]s resided. For this reason, {{ill|Shimenawa|en|Shimenawa|WD=Q1887421|lt=Shimenawa|1=Shimenawa}}s and [[torii]]s were decorated as proof that a deity resided there (kanzumaru).
It is also an embodiment of the {{ill|Concept|en|Concept|WD=Q151885|lt=Concept|1=Concept}} of the two sides of the same coin that pervades ancient Shinto and current [[shinto]]s, such as the idea that this world consists of Utsushi-yo and Tokoyo, and the [[Seven Lucky Gods]] of {{ill|Ebisu (mythology)|en|Ebisu (mythology)|WD=Q1129330|lt=Ebisu|1=Ebisu (mythology)}} and Daikoku, two of the [[Seven Lucky Gods]], are believed to be one, and the counting of {{ill|Chopsticks|en|Chopsticks|WD=Q81980|lt=Chopsticks|1=Chopsticks}} and {{ill|footwear|en|footwear|WD=Q161928|lt=footwear|1=Footwear}} as one set or one pair is also said to be unique to Japan.
In the [[Kojiki]], there are many [[:en:myths|myths]] about married couples, from {{ill|Izanami|en|Izanami|WD=Q682306|lt=Izanami|1=Izanami}} and [[Izanagi]] to [[Sarutahiko Ōkami]] and [[Ame-no-Uzume]]. It is thought that these became {{ill|Dōsojin|en|Dōsojin|WD=Q269515|lt=Sai no Kami|1=Dōsojin}} and {{ill|Dōsojin|en|Dōsojin|WD=Q269515|lt=Dosojin|1=Dōsojin}}, and were connected with the belief in a rock formation. This is why {{ill|Kṣitigarbha|en|Kṣitigarbha|WD=Q604687|lt=Jizo|1=Kṣitigarbha}}s and Dōsojin are often depicted as a couple or as a pair of large and small rocks or stone statues. This kind of belief in married couples has spread throughout the world over time and has become familiar in the form of married couple's bowls, etc. At the same time, it is deeply related to the belief in child-rearing and child-bearing in the framework of {{ill|Family|en|Family|WD=Q8436|lt=Family|1=Family}}, such as {{ill|Ie (Japanese family system)|en|Ie (Japanese family system)|WD=Q1149315|lt=householder|1=Ie (Japanese family system)}} and home. The '<nowiki/>'''Iwana'''' are deeply related to the belief in child-bearing, child-rearing, and the treasure of children.
These ideas of '''rock-building belief''', '''Omote-Taiwanai''' and '''matrimonial belief''' (also called matrimonial harmony, which is the basis of {{ill|Veneration of the dead|en|Veneration of the dead|WD=Q238199|lt=ancestral spirit belief|1=Veneration of the dead}}) are combined to form the object of enshrinement at the couple's rock.
== Oshimenawa == An example of an '''oshimenawa''' is Tateishi in {{ill|Futami, Mie|en|Futami, Mie|WD=Q5510468|lt=Futami Town|1=Futami, Mie}}, Ise City, Mie Prefecture. The large {{ill|Shimenawa|en|Shimenawa|WD=Q1887421|lt=Shimenawa|1=Shimenawa}} rope connecting Tateishi and Nejiriwa, known as "husband and wife rocks," is believed to be the torii (gateway) to the offshore Kohtama Shrine stone, and is reattached three times a year in December (before the New Year), May, and September.<ref>[http://www.jingukaikan.jp/sukeikai/imgs_mimosuso/41.pdf Special Feature: Shimenawa at Ise] Jingu Kaikan reverence association</ref> During the shimenawa-renawa-renawa-renawa-renawa-renawa-renawa-renawa ceremony, a woodcarving song is sung, and some people take pieces of the old rope home as a good-luck charm for marital bliss.<ref>[http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mX_b2p0j14U husband-and-wife-iwa-dai-shimenawa-renawa-renawa-renawa-renawa-shikiji] Youtube 2010/12/19</ref>
== Influence == American composer {{ill|Roger Reynolds|en|Roger Reynolds|WD=Q673278|lt=Roger Reynolds|1=Roger Reynolds}} took reference to the form of Meoto Iwa in Futami, where he visited in 1966, while composing the first movement "''Futami ga Ura''" of his second symphony, "''Symphony [Myths]''" (1990). Divided into 3 sections, the first and the last with "densely stratified texture" represent Izanagi and Izanami rocks respectively, and the middle section represents the space in-between.<ref>{{cite thesis |type=PhD |last=Summar |first=Sarah Page |date=December 2012 |title=Fidget, Sway, and Swerve: Three Works Inspired by Movement from the Intricate Maneuvers Series |publisher=University of North Texas |url=https://digital.library.unt.edu/ark%3A/67531/metadc177259/m2/1/high_res_d/dissertation.pdf}}</ref>
== National Married Couple Rocks Summit == The '''National Married Couple Rocks Summit Liaison Council''' has been formed by 10 tourist spots in Japan that have married couple rocks or rocks for married couples, and is holding the National Married Couple Rocks Summit.

{{Short description|Type of sacred rocks in Shinto}} {{distinguish|Meoto Rocks}} {{more citations needed|date=April 2022}}{{Split|date=June 2022|Meoto Iwa (Ise)|Meoto Iwa Rocks|discuss=Talk:Meoto Iwa#Split proposal}}[[File:Meotoiwa.jpg|right|thumb|250x250px|Meoto Iwa, the wedded rocks, daytime]] [[File:Meoto_Iwa_at_dusk.jpg|right|thumb|Meoto Iwa, the wedded rocks, at dusk]] {{nihongo|'''Meoto Iwa'''|夫婦岩}}, or '''Married Couple Rocks''', are a kind of rock formation seen as religiously significant in [[Shinto]]. They are a subtype of [[Iwakura rock]].
According to [[Shinto]], the rocks represent the union of the creator ''[[kami]]'', [[Izanagi]] and {{ill|Izanami|en|Izanami|WD=Q682306|lt=Izanami|1=Izanami}}. The rocks, therefore, celebrate the union in marriage of man and woman.
The most famous pair is the pair at [[Futami Okitama Shrine]] in [[:en:Futami-ura|Futami-ura]], two rocky [[:en:Stack (Geology)|stacks]] off the coast from {{ill|Ise, Mie|en|Ise, Mie|WD=Q328067|lt=Ise, Mie|1=Ise, Mie}}, {{ill|Japan|en|Japan|WD=Q17|lt=Japan|1=Japan}}. They are joined by a ''{{ill|Shimenawa|en|Shimenawa|WD=Q1887421|lt=Shimenawa|1=Shimenawa}}'' (a heavy rope of rice straw) and are considered sacred by worshippers of the shrine. The shimenawa, composed of five separate strands which each weigh 40 kilograms,<ref>{{cite web |title=Meoto-iwa rocks (Mie Prefecture) - Let's travel around Japan! |url=http://www.travel-around-japan.com/k54-07-meoto-iwa.html |access-date=13 March 2021 |website=Let's travel around Japan}}</ref> must be replaced several times a year in a special ceremony. The larger rock, said to be male, has a small ''[[torii]]'' at its peak.[[File:Hiroshige,_Futamigaura_in_Ise_Province,_1858.jpg|thumb|Fuji 36 Views of Ise Futamikaura" by [[:en:Hiroshige Utagawa|Hiroshige Utagawa]].]]At dawn during the summer, the sun appears to rise between the two rocks. {{ill|Mount Fuji|en|Mount Fuji|WD=Q39231|lt=Mount Fuji|1=Mount Fuji}} is visible in the distance. At low tide, the rocks are not separated by water.
[[Futami Okitama Shrine|Okitama Shrine]] is dedicated to [[Sarutahiko Ōkami]] and imperial food goddess [[Ukanomitama]]. There are numerous statues of frogs around the shrine. The shrine and the two rocks are near the [[:en:Grand Shrine of Ise|Grand Shrine of Ise]], the most important location of [[Misogi|purification]] in Shinto.
== Outline == The couple rocks at [[Futami Okitama Shrine]] in {{ill|Mie Prefecture|en|Mie Prefecture|WD=Q128196|lt=Mie Prefecture|1=Mie Prefecture}} {{ill|Ise, Mie|en|Ise, Mie|WD=Q328067|lt=Ise City|1=Ise, Mie}} have been known for a long time, as depicted by {{ill|Ukiyo-e artist|ja|浮世絵師|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ukiyo-e artist|1=ukiyo-e artist|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q33082999}} in the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period|1=Edo period}}, and are generally used as a symbol and prayer for marital bliss and domestic safety, maritime security and great catch, and is said to be a symbol of [[Iwakura rock|Iwakura Shinko]] in [[Ko-Shintō|Kojindo]], which means a symbolic place or object in {{ill|Nature|en|Nature|WD=Q7860|lt=Nature|1=Nature}}, especially megaliths, {{ill|Rock (geology)|en|Rock (geology)|WD=Q8063|lt=rocks|1=Rock (geology)}}, and {{ill|Mountain|en|Mountain|WD=Q8502|lt=Mountain|1=Mountain}}s, were considered [[Shintai]]s and believed to be places where [[Kami]]s resided. For this reason, {{ill|Shimenawa|en|Shimenawa|WD=Q1887421|lt=Shimenawa|1=Shimenawa}}s and [[torii]]s were decorated as proof that a deity resided there (kanzumaru).
It is also an embodiment of the {{ill|Concept|en|Concept|WD=Q151885|lt=Concept|1=Concept}} of the two sides of the same coin that pervades ancient Shinto and current [[shinto]]s, such as the idea that this world consists of Utsushi-yo and Tokoyo, and the [[Seven Lucky Gods]] of {{ill|Ebisu (mythology)|en|Ebisu (mythology)|WD=Q1129330|lt=Ebisu|1=Ebisu (mythology)}} and Daikoku, two of the [[Seven Lucky Gods]], are believed to be one, and the counting of {{ill|Chopsticks|en|Chopsticks|WD=Q81980|lt=Chopsticks|1=Chopsticks}} and {{ill|footwear|en|footwear|WD=Q161928|lt=footwear|1=Footwear}} as one set or one pair is also said to be unique to Japan.
In the [[Kojiki]], there are many [[:en:myths|myths]] about married couples, from {{ill|Izanami|en|Izanami|WD=Q682306|lt=Izanami|1=Izanami}} and [[Izanagi]] to [[Sarutahiko Ōkami]] and [[Ame-no-Uzume]]. It is thought that these became {{ill|Dōsojin|en|Dōsojin|WD=Q269515|lt=Sai no Kami|1=Dōsojin}} and {{ill|Dōsojin|en|Dōsojin|WD=Q269515|lt=Dosojin|1=Dōsojin}}, and were connected with the belief in a rock formation. This is why {{ill|Kṣitigarbha|en|Kṣitigarbha|WD=Q604687|lt=Jizo|1=Kṣitigarbha}}s and Dōsojin are often depicted as a couple or as a pair of large and small rocks or stone statues. This kind of belief in married couples has spread throughout the world over time and has become familiar in the form of married couple's bowls, etc. At the same time, it is deeply related to the belief in child-rearing and child-bearing in the framework of {{ill|Family|en|Family|WD=Q8436|lt=Family|1=Family}}, such as {{ill|Ie (Japanese family system)|en|Ie (Japanese family system)|WD=Q1149315|lt=householder|1=Ie (Japanese family system)}} and home. The '<nowiki/>'''Iwana'''' are deeply related to the belief in child-bearing, child-rearing, and the treasure of children.
These ideas of '''rock-building belief''', '''Omote-Taiwanai''' and '''matrimonial belief''' (also called matrimonial harmony, which is the basis of {{ill|Veneration of the dead|en|Veneration of the dead|WD=Q238199|lt=ancestral spirit belief|1=Veneration of the dead}}) are combined to form the object of enshrinement at the couple's rock.
== Oshimenawa == An example of an '''oshimenawa''' is Tateishi in {{ill|Futami, Mie|en|Futami, Mie|WD=Q5510468|lt=Futami Town|1=Futami, Mie}}, Ise City, Mie Prefecture. The large {{ill|Shimenawa|en|Shimenawa|WD=Q1887421|lt=Shimenawa|1=Shimenawa}} rope connecting Tateishi and Nejiriwa, known as "husband and wife rocks," is believed to be the torii (gateway) to the offshore Kohtama Shrine stone, and is reattached three times a year in December (before the New Year), May, and September.<ref>[http://www.jingukaikan.jp/sukeikai/imgs_mimosuso/41.pdf Special Feature: Shimenawa at Ise] Jingu Kaikan reverence association</ref> During the shimenawa-renawa-renawa-renawa-renawa-renawa-renawa-renawa ceremony, a woodcarving song is sung, and some people take pieces of the old rope home as a good-luck charm for marital bliss.<ref>[http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mX_b2p0j14U husband-and-wife-iwa-dai-shimenawa-renawa-renawa-renawa-renawa-shikiji] Youtube 2010/12/19</ref>
== Influence == American composer {{ill|Roger Reynolds|en|Roger Reynolds|WD=Q673278|lt=Roger Reynolds|1=Roger Reynolds}} took reference to the form of Meoto Iwa in Futami, where he visited in 1966, while composing the first movement "''Futami ga Ura''" of his second symphony, "''Symphony [Myths]''" (1990). Divided into 3 sections, the first and the last with "densely stratified texture" represent Izanagi and Izanami rocks respectively, and the middle section represents the space in-between.<ref>{{cite thesis |type=PhD |last=Summar |first=Sarah Page |date=December 2012 |title=Fidget, Sway, and Swerve: Three Works Inspired by Movement from the Intricate Maneuvers Series |publisher=University of North Texas |url=https://digital.library.unt.edu/ark%3A/67531/metadc177259/m2/1/high_res_d/dissertation.pdf}}</ref>
== National Married Couple Rocks Summit == The '''National Married Couple Rocks Summit Liaison Council''' has been formed by 10 tourist spots in Japan that have married couple rocks or rocks for married couples, and is holding the National Married Couple Rocks Summit.

{{Short description|Type of sacred rocks in Shinto}} {{distinguish|Meoto Rocks}} {{more citations needed|date=April 2022}}{{Split|date=June 2022|Meoto Iwa (Ise)|Meoto Iwa Rocks|discuss=Talk:Meoto Iwa#Split proposal}}[[File:Meotoiwa.jpg|right|thumb|250x250px|Meoto Iwa, the wedded rocks, daytime]] [[File:Meoto_Iwa_at_dusk.jpg|right|thumb|Meoto Iwa, the wedded rocks, at dusk]] {{nihongo|'''Meoto Iwa'''|夫婦岩}}, or '''Married Couple Rocks''', are a kind of rock formation seen as religiously significant in [[Shinto]]. They are a subtype of [[Iwakura rock]].
According to [[Shinto]], the rocks represent the union of the creator ''[[kami]]'', [[Izanagi]] and {{ill|Izanami|en|Izanami|WD=Q682306|lt=Izanami|1=Izanami}}. The rocks, therefore, celebrate the union in marriage of man and woman.
The most famous pair is the pair at [[Futami Okitama Shrine]] in [[:en:Futami-ura|Futami-ura]], two rocky [[:en:Stack (Geology)|stacks]] off the coast from {{ill|Ise, Mie|en|Ise, Mie|WD=Q328067|lt=Ise, Mie|1=Ise, Mie}}, {{ill|Japan|en|Japan|WD=Q17|lt=Japan|1=Japan}}. They are joined by a ''{{ill|Shimenawa|en|Shimenawa|WD=Q1887421|lt=Shimenawa|1=Shimenawa}}'' (a heavy rope of rice straw) and are considered sacred by worshippers of the shrine. The shimenawa, composed of five separate strands which each weigh 40 kilograms,<ref>{{cite web |title=Meoto-iwa rocks (Mie Prefecture) - Let's travel around Japan! |url=http://www.travel-around-japan.com/k54-07-meoto-iwa.html |access-date=13 March 2021 |website=Let's travel around Japan}}</ref> must be replaced several times a year in a special ceremony. The larger rock, said to be male, has a small ''[[torii]]'' at its peak.[[File:Hiroshige,_Futamigaura_in_Ise_Province,_1858.jpg|thumb|Fuji 36 Views of Ise Futamikaura" by [[:en:Hiroshige Utagawa|Hiroshige Utagawa]].]]At dawn during the summer, the sun appears to rise between the two rocks. {{ill|Mount Fuji|en|Mount Fuji|WD=Q39231|lt=Mount Fuji|1=Mount Fuji}} is visible in the distance. At low tide, the rocks are not separated by water.
[[Futami Okitama Shrine|Okitama Shrine]] is dedicated to [[Sarutahiko Ōkami]] and imperial food goddess [[Ukanomitama]]. There are numerous statues of frogs around the shrine. The shrine and the two rocks are near the [[:en:Grand Shrine of Ise|Grand Shrine of Ise]], the most important location of [[Misogi|purification]] in Shinto.
== Outline == The couple rocks at [[Futami Okitama Shrine]] in {{ill|Mie Prefecture|en|Mie Prefecture|WD=Q128196|lt=Mie Prefecture|1=Mie Prefecture}} {{ill|Ise, Mie|en|Ise, Mie|WD=Q328067|lt=Ise City|1=Ise, Mie}} have been known for a long time, as depicted by {{ill|Ukiyo-e artist|ja|浮世絵師|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ukiyo-e artist|1=ukiyo-e artist|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q33082999}} in the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period|1=Edo period}}, and are generally used as a symbol and prayer for marital bliss and domestic safety, maritime security and great catch, and is said to be a symbol of [[Iwakura rock|Iwakura Shinko]] in [[Ko-Shintō|Kojindo]], which means a symbolic place or object in {{ill|Nature|en|Nature|WD=Q7860|lt=Nature|1=Nature}}, especially megaliths, {{ill|Rock (geology)|en|Rock (geology)|WD=Q8063|lt=rocks|1=Rock (geology)}}, and {{ill|Mountain|en|Mountain|WD=Q8502|lt=Mountain|1=Mountain}}s, were considered [[Shintai]]s and believed to be places where [[Kami]]s resided. For this reason, {{ill|Shimenawa|en|Shimenawa|WD=Q1887421|lt=Shimenawa|1=Shimenawa}}s and [[torii]]s were decorated as proof that a deity resided there (kanzumaru).
It is also an embodiment of the {{ill|Concept|en|Concept|WD=Q151885|lt=Concept|1=Concept}} of the two sides of the same coin that pervades ancient Shinto and current [[shinto]]s, such as the idea that this world consists of Utsushi-yo and Tokoyo, and the [[Seven Lucky Gods]] of {{ill|Ebisu (mythology)|en|Ebisu (mythology)|WD=Q1129330|lt=Ebisu|1=Ebisu (mythology)}} and Daikoku, two of the [[Seven Lucky Gods]], are believed to be one, and the counting of {{ill|Chopsticks|en|Chopsticks|WD=Q81980|lt=Chopsticks|1=Chopsticks}} and {{ill|footwear|en|footwear|WD=Q161928|lt=footwear|1=Footwear}} as one set or one pair is also said to be unique to Japan.
In the [[Kojiki]], there are many [[:en:myths|myths]] about married couples, from {{ill|Izanami|en|Izanami|WD=Q682306|lt=Izanami|1=Izanami}} and [[Izanagi]] to [[Sarutahiko Ōkami]] and [[Ame-no-Uzume]]. It is thought that these became {{ill|Dōsojin|en|Dōsojin|WD=Q269515|lt=Sai no Kami|1=Dōsojin}} and {{ill|Dōsojin|en|Dōsojin|WD=Q269515|lt=Dosojin|1=Dōsojin}}, and were connected with the belief in a rock formation. This is why {{ill|Kṣitigarbha|en|Kṣitigarbha|WD=Q604687|lt=Jizo|1=Kṣitigarbha}}s and Dōsojin are often depicted as a couple or as a pair of large and small rocks or stone statues. This kind of belief in married couples has spread throughout the world over time and has become familiar in the form of married couple's bowls, etc. At the same time, it is deeply related to the belief in child-rearing and child-bearing in the framework of {{ill|Family|en|Family|WD=Q8436|lt=Family|1=Family}}, such as {{ill|Ie (Japanese family system)|en|Ie (Japanese family system)|WD=Q1149315|lt=householder|1=Ie (Japanese family system)}} and home. The '<nowiki/>'''Iwana'''' are deeply related to the belief in child-bearing, child-rearing, and the treasure of children.
These ideas of '''rock-building belief''', '''Omote-Taiwanai''' and '''matrimonial belief''' (also called matrimonial harmony, which is the basis of {{ill|Veneration of the dead|en|Veneration of the dead|WD=Q238199|lt=ancestral spirit belief|1=Veneration of the dead}}) are combined to form the object of enshrinement at the couple's rock.
== Oshimenawa == An example of an '''oshimenawa''' is Tateishi in {{ill|Futami, Mie|en|Futami, Mie|WD=Q5510468|lt=Futami Town|1=Futami, Mie}}, Ise City, Mie Prefecture. The large {{ill|Shimenawa|en|Shimenawa|WD=Q1887421|lt=Shimenawa|1=Shimenawa}} rope connecting Tateishi and Nejiriwa, known as "husband and wife rocks," is believed to be the torii (gateway) to the offshore Kohtama Shrine stone, and is reattached three times a year in December (before the New Year), May, and September.<ref>[http://www.jingukaikan.jp/sukeikai/imgs_mimosuso/41.pdf Special Feature: Shimenawa at Ise] Jingu Kaikan reverence association</ref> During the shimenawa-renawa-renawa-renawa-renawa-renawa-renawa-renawa ceremony, a woodcarving song is sung, and some people take pieces of the old rope home as a good-luck charm for marital bliss.<ref>[http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mX_b2p0j14U husband-and-wife-iwa-dai-shimenawa-renawa-renawa-renawa-renawa-shikiji] Youtube 2010/12/19</ref>
== Influence == American composer {{ill|Roger Reynolds|en|Roger Reynolds|WD=Q673278|lt=Roger Reynolds|1=Roger Reynolds}} took reference to the form of Meoto Iwa in Futami, where he visited in 1966, while composing the first movement "''Futami ga Ura''" of his second symphony, "''Symphony [Myths]''" (1990). Divided into 3 sections, the first and the last with "densely stratified texture" represent Izanagi and Izanami rocks respectively, and the middle section represents the space in-between.<ref>{{cite thesis |type=PhD |last=Summar |first=Sarah Page |date=December 2012 |title=Fidget, Sway, and Swerve: Three Works Inspired by Movement from the Intricate Maneuvers Series |publisher=University of North Texas |url=https://digital.library.unt.edu/ark%3A/67531/metadc177259/m2/1/high_res_d/dissertation.pdf}}</ref>
== National Married Couple Rocks Summit == The '''National Married Couple Rocks Summit Liaison Council''' has been formed by 10 tourist spots in Japan that have married couple rocks or rocks for married couples, and is holding the National Married Couple Rocks Summit.

{{Short description|Type of sacred rocks in Shinto}} {{distinguish|Meoto Rocks}} {{more citations needed|date=April 2022}}{{Split|date=June 2022|Meoto Iwa (Ise)|Meoto Iwa Rocks|discuss=Talk:Meoto Iwa#Split proposal}}[[File:Meotoiwa.jpg|right|thumb|250x250px|Meoto Iwa, the wedded rocks, daytime]] [[File:Meoto_Iwa_at_dusk.jpg|right|thumb|Meoto Iwa, the wedded rocks, at dusk]] {{nihongo|'''Meoto Iwa'''|夫婦岩}}, or '''Married Couple Rocks''', are a kind of rock formation seen as religiously significant in [[Shinto]]. They are a subtype of [[Iwakura rock]].
According to [[Shinto]], the rocks represent the union of the creator ''[[kami]]'', [[Izanagi]] and {{ill|Izanami|en|Izanami|WD=Q682306|lt=Izanami|1=Izanami}}. The rocks, therefore, celebrate the union in marriage of man and woman.
The most famous pair is the pair at [[Futami Okitama Shrine]] in [[:en:Futami-ura|Futami-ura]], two rocky [[:en:Stack (Geology)|stacks]] off the coast from {{ill|Ise, Mie|en|Ise, Mie|WD=Q328067|lt=Ise, Mie|1=Ise, Mie}}, {{ill|Japan|en|Japan|WD=Q17|lt=Japan|1=Japan}}. They are joined by a ''{{ill|Shimenawa|en|Shimenawa|WD=Q1887421|lt=Shimenawa|1=Shimenawa}}'' (a heavy rope of rice straw) and are considered sacred by worshippers of the shrine. The shimenawa, composed of five separate strands which each weigh 40 kilograms,<ref>{{cite web |title=Meoto-iwa rocks (Mie Prefecture) - Let's travel around Japan! |url=http://www.travel-around-japan.com/k54-07-meoto-iwa.html |access-date=13 March 2021 |website=Let's travel around Japan}}</ref> must be replaced several times a year in a special ceremony. The larger rock, said to be male, has a small ''[[torii]]'' at its peak.[[File:Hiroshige,_Futamigaura_in_Ise_Province,_1858.jpg|thumb|Fuji 36 Views of Ise Futamikaura" by [[:en:Hiroshige Utagawa|Hiroshige Utagawa]].]]At dawn during the summer, the sun appears to rise between the two rocks. {{ill|Mount Fuji|en|Mount Fuji|WD=Q39231|lt=Mount Fuji|1=Mount Fuji}} is visible in the distance. At low tide, the rocks are not separated by water.
[[Futami Okitama Shrine|Okitama Shrine]] is dedicated to [[Sarutahiko Ōkami]] and imperial food goddess [[Ukanomitama]]. There are numerous statues of frogs around the shrine. The shrine and the two rocks are near the [[:en:Grand Shrine of Ise|Grand Shrine of Ise]], the most important location of [[Misogi|purification]] in Shinto.
== Outline == The couple rocks at [[Futami Okitama Shrine]] in {{ill|Mie Prefecture|en|Mie Prefecture|WD=Q128196|lt=Mie Prefecture|1=Mie Prefecture}} {{ill|Ise, Mie|en|Ise, Mie|WD=Q328067|lt=Ise City|1=Ise, Mie}} have been known for a long time, as depicted by {{ill|Ukiyo-e artist|ja|浮世絵師|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ukiyo-e artist|1=ukiyo-e artist|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q33082999}} in the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period|1=Edo period}}, and are generally used as a symbol and prayer for marital bliss and domestic safety, maritime security and great catch, and is said to be a symbol of [[Iwakura rock|Iwakura Shinko]] in [[Ko-Shintō|Kojindo]], which means a symbolic place or object in {{ill|Nature|en|Nature|WD=Q7860|lt=Nature|1=Nature}}, especially megaliths, {{ill|Rock (geology)|en|Rock (geology)|WD=Q8063|lt=rocks|1=Rock (geology)}}, and {{ill|Mountain|en|Mountain|WD=Q8502|lt=Mountain|1=Mountain}}s, were considered [[Shintai]]s and believed to be places where [[Kami]]s resided. For this reason, {{ill|Shimenawa|en|Shimenawa|WD=Q1887421|lt=Shimenawa|1=Shimenawa}}s and [[torii]]s were decorated as proof that a deity resided there (kanzumaru).
It is also an embodiment of the {{ill|Concept|en|Concept|WD=Q151885|lt=Concept|1=Concept}} of the two sides of the same coin that pervades ancient Shinto and current [[shinto]]s, such as the idea that this world consists of Utsushi-yo and Tokoyo, and the [[Seven Lucky Gods]] of {{ill|Ebisu (mythology)|en|Ebisu (mythology)|WD=Q1129330|lt=Ebisu|1=Ebisu (mythology)}} and Daikoku, two of the [[Seven Lucky Gods]], are believed to be one, and the counting of {{ill|Chopsticks|en|Chopsticks|WD=Q81980|lt=Chopsticks|1=Chopsticks}} and {{ill|footwear|en|footwear|WD=Q161928|lt=footwear|1=Footwear}} as one set or one pair is also said to be unique to Japan.
In the [[Kojiki]], there are many [[:en:myths|myths]] about married couples, from {{ill|Izanami|en|Izanami|WD=Q682306|lt=Izanami|1=Izanami}} and [[Izanagi]] to [[Sarutahiko Ōkami]] and [[Ame-no-Uzume]]. It is thought that these became {{ill|Dōsojin|en|Dōsojin|WD=Q269515|lt=Sai no Kami|1=Dōsojin}} and {{ill|Dōsojin|en|Dōsojin|WD=Q269515|lt=Dosojin|1=Dōsojin}}, and were connected with the belief in a rock formation. This is why {{ill|Kṣitigarbha|en|Kṣitigarbha|WD=Q604687|lt=Jizo|1=Kṣitigarbha}}s and Dōsojin are often depicted as a couple or as a pair of large and small rocks or stone statues. This kind of belief in married couples has spread throughout the world over time and has become familiar in the form of married couple's bowls, etc. At the same time, it is deeply related to the belief in child-rearing and child-bearing in the framework of {{ill|Family|en|Family|WD=Q8436|lt=Family|1=Family}}, such as {{ill|Ie (Japanese family system)|en|Ie (Japanese family system)|WD=Q1149315|lt=householder|1=Ie (Japanese family system)}} and home. The '<nowiki/>'''Iwana'''' are deeply related to the belief in child-bearing, child-rearing, and the treasure of children.
These ideas of '''rock-building belief''', '''Omote-Taiwanai''' and '''matrimonial belief''' (also called matrimonial harmony, which is the basis of {{ill|Veneration of the dead|en|Veneration of the dead|WD=Q238199|lt=ancestral spirit belief|1=Veneration of the dead}}) are combined to form the object of enshrinement at the couple's rock.
== Oshimenawa == An example of an '''oshimenawa''' is Tateishi in {{ill|Futami, Mie|en|Futami, Mie|WD=Q5510468|lt=Futami Town|1=Futami, Mie}}, Ise City, Mie Prefecture. The large {{ill|Shimenawa|en|Shimenawa|WD=Q1887421|lt=Shimenawa|1=Shimenawa}} rope connecting Tateishi and Nejiriwa, known as "husband and wife rocks," is believed to be the torii (gateway) to the offshore Kohtama Shrine stone, and is reattached three times a year in December (before the New Year), May, and September.<ref>[http://www.jingukaikan.jp/sukeikai/imgs_mimosuso/41.pdf Special Feature: Shimenawa at Ise] Jingu Kaikan reverence association</ref> During the shimenawa-renawa-renawa-renawa-renawa-renawa-renawa-renawa ceremony, a woodcarving song is sung, and some people take pieces of the old rope home as a good-luck charm for marital bliss.<ref>[http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mX_b2p0j14U husband-and-wife-iwa-dai-shimenawa-renawa-renawa-renawa-renawa-shikiji] Youtube 2010/12/19</ref>
== Influence == American composer {{ill|Roger Reynolds|en|Roger Reynolds|WD=Q673278|lt=Roger Reynolds|1=Roger Reynolds}} took reference to the form of Meoto Iwa in Futami, where he visited in 1966, while composing the first movement "''Futami ga Ura''" of his second symphony, "''Symphony [Myths]''" (1990). Divided into 3 sections, the first and the last with "densely stratified texture" represent Izanagi and Izanami rocks respectively, and the middle section represents the space in-between.<ref>{{cite thesis |type=PhD |last=Summar |first=Sarah Page |date=December 2012 |title=Fidget, Sway, and Swerve: Three Works Inspired by Movement from the Intricate Maneuvers Series |publisher=University of North Texas |url=https://digital.library.unt.edu/ark%3A/67531/metadc177259/m2/1/high_res_d/dissertation.pdf}}</ref>
== National Married Couple Rocks Summit == The '''National Married Couple Rocks Summit Liaison Council''' has been formed by 10 tourist spots in Japan that have married couple rocks or rocks for married couples, and is holding the National Married Couple Rocks Summit.

{{Short description|Type of sacred rocks in Shinto}} {{distinguish|Meoto Rocks}} {{more citations needed|date=April 2022}}{{Split|date=June 2022|Meoto Iwa (Ise)|Meoto Iwa Rocks|discuss=Talk:Meoto Iwa#Split proposal}}[[File:Meotoiwa.jpg|right|thumb|250x250px|Meoto Iwa, the wedded rocks, daytime]] [[File:Meoto_Iwa_at_dusk.jpg|right|thumb|Meoto Iwa, the wedded rocks, at dusk]] {{nihongo|'''Meoto Iwa'''|夫婦岩}}, or '''Married Couple Rocks''', are a kind of rock formation seen as religiously significant in [[Shinto]]. They are a subtype of [[Iwakura rock]].
According to [[Shinto]], the rocks represent the union of the creator ''[[kami]]'', [[Izanagi]] and {{ill|Izanami|en|Izanami|WD=Q682306|lt=Izanami|1=Izanami}}. The rocks, therefore, celebrate the union in marriage of man and woman.
The most famous pair is the pair at [[Futami Okitama Shrine]] in [[:en:Futami-ura|Futami-ura]], two rocky [[:en:Stack (Geology)|stacks]] off the coast from {{ill|Ise, Mie|en|Ise, Mie|WD=Q328067|lt=Ise, Mie|1=Ise, Mie}}, {{ill|Japan|en|Japan|WD=Q17|lt=Japan|1=Japan}}. They are joined by a ''{{ill|Shimenawa|en|Shimenawa|WD=Q1887421|lt=Shimenawa|1=Shimenawa}}'' (a heavy rope of rice straw) and are considered sacred by worshippers of the shrine. The shimenawa, composed of five separate strands which each weigh 40 kilograms,<ref>{{cite web |title=Meoto-iwa rocks (Mie Prefecture) - Let's travel around Japan! |url=http://www.travel-around-japan.com/k54-07-meoto-iwa.html |access-date=13 March 2021 |website=Let's travel around Japan}}</ref> must be replaced several times a year in a special ceremony. The larger rock, said to be male, has a small ''[[torii]]'' at its peak.[[File:Hiroshige,_Futamigaura_in_Ise_Province,_1858.jpg|thumb|Fuji 36 Views of Ise Futamikaura" by [[:en:Hiroshige Utagawa|Hiroshige Utagawa]].]]At dawn during the summer, the sun appears to rise between the two rocks. {{ill|Mount Fuji|en|Mount Fuji|WD=Q39231|lt=Mount Fuji|1=Mount Fuji}} is visible in the distance. At low tide, the rocks are not separated by water.
[[Futami Okitama Shrine|Okitama Shrine]] is dedicated to [[Sarutahiko Ōkami]] and imperial food goddess [[Ukanomitama]]. There are numerous statues of frogs around the shrine. The shrine and the two rocks are near the [[:en:Grand Shrine of Ise|Grand Shrine of Ise]], the most important location of [[Misogi|purification]] in Shinto.
== Outline == The couple rocks at [[Futami Okitama Shrine]] in {{ill|Mie Prefecture|en|Mie Prefecture|WD=Q128196|lt=Mie Prefecture|1=Mie Prefecture}} {{ill|Ise, Mie|en|Ise, Mie|WD=Q328067|lt=Ise City|1=Ise, Mie}} have been known for a long time, as depicted by {{ill|Ukiyo-e artist|ja|浮世絵師|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ukiyo-e artist|1=ukiyo-e artist|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q33082999}} in the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period|1=Edo period}}, and are generally used as a symbol and prayer for marital bliss and domestic safety, maritime security and great catch, and is said to be a symbol of [[Iwakura rock|Iwakura Shinko]] in [[Ko-Shintō|Kojindo]], which means a symbolic place or object in {{ill|Nature|en|Nature|WD=Q7860|lt=Nature|1=Nature}}, especially megaliths, {{ill|Rock (geology)|en|Rock (geology)|WD=Q8063|lt=rocks|1=Rock (geology)}}, and {{ill|Mountain|en|Mountain|WD=Q8502|lt=Mountain|1=Mountain}}s, were considered [[Shintai]]s and believed to be places where [[Kami]]s resided. For this reason, {{ill|Shimenawa|en|Shimenawa|WD=Q1887421|lt=Shimenawa|1=Shimenawa}}s and [[torii]]s were decorated as proof that a deity resided there (kanzumaru).
It is also an embodiment of the {{ill|Concept|en|Concept|WD=Q151885|lt=Concept|1=Concept}} of the two sides of the same coin that pervades ancient Shinto and current [[shinto]]s, such as the idea that this world consists of Utsushi-yo and Tokoyo, and the [[Seven Lucky Gods]] of {{ill|Ebisu (mythology)|en|Ebisu (mythology)|WD=Q1129330|lt=Ebisu|1=Ebisu (mythology)}} and Daikoku, two of the [[Seven Lucky Gods]], are believed to be one, and the counting of {{ill|Chopsticks|en|Chopsticks|WD=Q81980|lt=Chopsticks|1=Chopsticks}} and {{ill|footwear|en|footwear|WD=Q161928|lt=footwear|1=Footwear}} as one set or one pair is also said to be unique to Japan.
In the [[Kojiki]], there are many [[:en:myths|myths]] about married couples, from {{ill|Izanami|en|Izanami|WD=Q682306|lt=Izanami|1=Izanami}} and [[Izanagi]] to [[Sarutahiko Ōkami]] and [[Ame-no-Uzume]]. It is thought that these became {{ill|Dōsojin|en|Dōsojin|WD=Q269515|lt=Sai no Kami|1=Dōsojin}} and {{ill|Dōsojin|en|Dōsojin|WD=Q269515|lt=Dosojin|1=Dōsojin}}, and were connected with the belief in a rock formation. This is why {{ill|Kṣitigarbha|en|Kṣitigarbha|WD=Q604687|lt=Jizo|1=Kṣitigarbha}}s and Dōsojin are often depicted as a couple or as a pair of large and small rocks or stone statues. This kind of belief in married couples has spread throughout the world over time and has become familiar in the form of married couple's bowls, etc. At the same time, it is deeply related to the belief in child-rearing and child-bearing in the framework of {{ill|Family|en|Family|WD=Q8436|lt=Family|1=Family}}, such as {{ill|Ie (Japanese family system)|en|Ie (Japanese family system)|WD=Q1149315|lt=householder|1=Ie (Japanese family system)}} and home. The '<nowiki/>'''Iwana'''' are deeply related to the belief in child-bearing, child-rearing, and the treasure of children.
These ideas of '''rock-building belief''', '''Omote-Taiwanai''' and '''matrimonial belief''' (also called matrimonial harmony, which is the basis of {{ill|Veneration of the dead|en|Veneration of the dead|WD=Q238199|lt=ancestral spirit belief|1=Veneration of the dead}}) are combined to form the object of enshrinement at the couple's rock.
== Oshimenawa == An example of an '''oshimenawa''' is Tateishi in {{ill|Futami, Mie|en|Futami, Mie|WD=Q5510468|lt=Futami Town|1=Futami, Mie}}, Ise City, Mie Prefecture. The large {{ill|Shimenawa|en|Shimenawa|WD=Q1887421|lt=Shimenawa|1=Shimenawa}} rope connecting Tateishi and Nejiriwa, known as "husband and wife rocks," is believed to be the torii (gateway) to the offshore Kohtama Shrine stone, and is reattached three times a year in December (before the New Year), May, and September.<ref>[http://www.jingukaikan.jp/sukeikai/imgs_mimosuso/41.pdf Special Feature: Shimenawa at Ise] Jingu Kaikan reverence association</ref> During the shimenawa-renawa-renawa-renawa-renawa-renawa-renawa-renawa ceremony, a woodcarving song is sung, and some people take pieces of the old rope home as a good-luck charm for marital bliss.<ref>[http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mX_b2p0j14U husband-and-wife-iwa-dai-shimenawa-renawa-renawa-renawa-renawa-shikiji] Youtube 2010/12/19</ref>
== Influence == American composer {{ill|Roger Reynolds|en|Roger Reynolds|WD=Q673278|lt=Roger Reynolds|1=Roger Reynolds}} took reference to the form of Meoto Iwa in Futami, where he visited in 1966, while composing the first movement "''Futami ga Ura''" of his second symphony, "''Symphony [Myths]''" (1990). Divided into 3 sections, the first and the last with "densely stratified texture" represent Izanagi and Izanami rocks respectively, and the middle section represents the space in-between.<ref>{{cite thesis |type=PhD |last=Summar |first=Sarah Page |date=December 2012 |title=Fidget, Sway, and Swerve: Three Works Inspired by Movement from the Intricate Maneuvers Series |publisher=University of North Texas |url=https://digital.library.unt.edu/ark%3A/67531/metadc177259/m2/1/high_res_d/dissertation.pdf}}</ref>
== National Married Couple Rocks Summit == The '''National Married Couple Rocks Summit Liaison Council''' has been formed by 10 tourist spots in Japan that have married couple rocks or rocks for married couples, and is holding the National Married Couple Rocks Summit.

{{Short description|Type of sacred rocks in Shinto}} {{distinguish|Meoto Rocks}} {{more citations needed|date=April 2022}}{{Split|date=June 2022|Meoto Iwa (Ise)|Meoto Iwa Rocks|discuss=Talk:Meoto Iwa#Split proposal}}[[File:Meotoiwa.jpg|right|thumb|250x250px|Meoto Iwa, the wedded rocks, daytime]] [[File:Meoto_Iwa_at_dusk.jpg|right|thumb|Meoto Iwa, the wedded rocks, at dusk]] {{nihongo|'''Meoto Iwa'''|夫婦岩}}, or '''Married Couple Rocks''', are a kind of rock formation seen as religiously significant in [[Shinto]]. They are a subtype of [[Iwakura rock]].
According to [[Shinto]], the rocks represent the union of the creator ''[[kami]]'', [[Izanagi]] and {{ill|Izanami|en|Izanami|WD=Q682306|lt=Izanami|1=Izanami}}. The rocks, therefore, celebrate the union in marriage of man and woman.
The most famous pair is the pair at [[Futami Okitama Shrine]] in [[:en:Futami-ura|Futami-ura]], two rocky [[:en:Stack (Geology)|stacks]] off the coast from {{ill|Ise, Mie|en|Ise, Mie|WD=Q328067|lt=Ise, Mie|1=Ise, Mie}}, {{ill|Japan|en|Japan|WD=Q17|lt=Japan|1=Japan}}. They are joined by a ''{{ill|Shimenawa|en|Shimenawa|WD=Q1887421|lt=Shimenawa|1=Shimenawa}}'' (a heavy rope of rice straw) and are considered sacred by worshippers of the shrine. The shimenawa, composed of five separate strands which each weigh 40 kilograms,<ref>{{cite web |title=Meoto-iwa rocks (Mie Prefecture) - Let's travel around Japan! |url=http://www.travel-around-japan.com/k54-07-meoto-iwa.html |access-date=13 March 2021 |website=Let's travel around Japan}}</ref> must be replaced several times a year in a special ceremony. The larger rock, said to be male, has a small ''[[torii]]'' at its peak.[[File:Hiroshige,_Futamigaura_in_Ise_Province,_1858.jpg|thumb|Fuji 36 Views of Ise Futamikaura" by [[:en:Hiroshige Utagawa|Hiroshige Utagawa]].]]At dawn during the summer, the sun appears to rise between the two rocks. {{ill|Mount Fuji|en|Mount Fuji|WD=Q39231|lt=Mount Fuji|1=Mount Fuji}} is visible in the distance. At low tide, the rocks are not separated by water.
[[Futami Okitama Shrine|Okitama Shrine]] is dedicated to [[Sarutahiko Ōkami]] and imperial food goddess [[Ukanomitama]]. There are numerous statues of frogs around the shrine. The shrine and the two rocks are near the [[:en:Grand Shrine of Ise|Grand Shrine of Ise]], the most important location of [[Misogi|purification]] in Shinto.
== Outline == The couple rocks at [[Futami Okitama Shrine]] in {{ill|Mie Prefecture|en|Mie Prefecture|WD=Q128196|lt=Mie Prefecture|1=Mie Prefecture}} {{ill|Ise, Mie|en|Ise, Mie|WD=Q328067|lt=Ise City|1=Ise, Mie}} have been known for a long time, as depicted by {{ill|Ukiyo-e artist|ja|浮世絵師|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ukiyo-e artist|1=ukiyo-e artist|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q33082999}} in the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period|1=Edo period}}, and are generally used as a symbol and prayer for marital bliss and domestic safety, maritime security and great catch, and is said to be a symbol of [[Iwakura rock|Iwakura Shinko]] in [[Ko-Shintō|Kojindo]], which means a symbolic place or object in {{ill|Nature|en|Nature|WD=Q7860|lt=Nature|1=Nature}}, especially megaliths, {{ill|Rock (geology)|en|Rock (geology)|WD=Q8063|lt=rocks|1=Rock (geology)}}, and {{ill|Mountain|en|Mountain|WD=Q8502|lt=Mountain|1=Mountain}}s, were considered [[Shintai]]s and believed to be places where [[Kami]]s resided. For this reason, {{ill|Shimenawa|en|Shimenawa|WD=Q1887421|lt=Shimenawa|1=Shimenawa}}s and [[torii]]s were decorated as proof that a deity resided there (kanzumaru).
It is also an embodiment of the {{ill|Concept|en|Concept|WD=Q151885|lt=Concept|1=Concept}} of the two sides of the same coin that pervades ancient Shinto and current [[shinto]]s, such as the idea that this world consists of Utsushi-yo and Tokoyo, and the [[Seven Lucky Gods]] of {{ill|Ebisu (mythology)|en|Ebisu (mythology)|WD=Q1129330|lt=Ebisu|1=Ebisu (mythology)}} and Daikoku, two of the [[Seven Lucky Gods]], are believed to be one, and the counting of {{ill|Chopsticks|en|Chopsticks|WD=Q81980|lt=Chopsticks|1=Chopsticks}} and {{ill|footwear|en|footwear|WD=Q161928|lt=footwear|1=Footwear}} as one set or one pair is also said to be unique to Japan.
In the [[Kojiki]], there are many [[:en:myths|myths]] about married couples, from {{ill|Izanami|en|Izanami|WD=Q682306|lt=Izanami|1=Izanami}} and [[Izanagi]] to [[Sarutahiko Ōkami]] and [[Ame-no-Uzume]]. It is thought that these became {{ill|Dōsojin|en|Dōsojin|WD=Q269515|lt=Sai no Kami|1=Dōsojin}} and {{ill|Dōsojin|en|Dōsojin|WD=Q269515|lt=Dosojin|1=Dōsojin}}, and were connected with the belief in a rock formation. This is why {{ill|Kṣitigarbha|en|Kṣitigarbha|WD=Q604687|lt=Jizo|1=Kṣitigarbha}}s and Dōsojin are often depicted as a couple or as a pair of large and small rocks or stone statues. This kind of belief in married couples has spread throughout the world over time and has become familiar in the form of married couple's bowls, etc. At the same time, it is deeply related to the belief in child-rearing and child-bearing in the framework of {{ill|Family|en|Family|WD=Q8436|lt=Family|1=Family}}, such as {{ill|Ie (Japanese family system)|en|Ie (Japanese family system)|WD=Q1149315|lt=householder|1=Ie (Japanese family system)}} and home. The '<nowiki/>'''Iwana'''' are deeply related to the belief in child-bearing, child-rearing, and the treasure of children.
These ideas of '''rock-building belief''', '''Omote-Taiwanai''' and '''matrimonial belief''' (also called matrimonial harmony, which is the basis of {{ill|Veneration of the dead|en|Veneration of the dead|WD=Q238199|lt=ancestral spirit belief|1=Veneration of the dead}}) are combined to form the object of enshrinement at the couple's rock.
== Oshimenawa == An example of an '''oshimenawa''' is Tateishi in {{ill|Futami, Mie|en|Futami, Mie|WD=Q5510468|lt=Futami Town|1=Futami, Mie}}, Ise City, Mie Prefecture. The large {{ill|Shimenawa|en|Shimenawa|WD=Q1887421|lt=Shimenawa|1=Shimenawa}} rope connecting Tateishi and Nejiriwa, known as "husband and wife rocks," is believed to be the torii (gateway) to the offshore Kohtama Shrine stone, and is reattached three times a year in December (before the New Year), May, and September.<ref>[http://www.jingukaikan.jp/sukeikai/imgs_mimosuso/41.pdf Special Feature: Shimenawa at Ise] Jingu Kaikan reverence association</ref> During the shimenawa-renawa-renawa-renawa-renawa-renawa-renawa-renawa ceremony, a woodcarving song is sung, and some people take pieces of the old rope home as a good-luck charm for marital bliss.<ref>[http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mX_b2p0j14U husband-and-wife-iwa-dai-shimenawa-renawa-renawa-renawa-renawa-shikiji] Youtube 2010/12/19</ref>
== Influence == American composer {{ill|Roger Reynolds|en|Roger Reynolds|WD=Q673278|lt=Roger Reynolds|1=Roger Reynolds}} took reference to the form of Meoto Iwa in Futami, where he visited in 1966, while composing the first movement "''Futami ga Ura''" of his second symphony, "''Symphony [Myths]''" (1990). Divided into 3 sections, the first and the last with "densely stratified texture" represent Izanagi and Izanami rocks respectively, and the middle section represents the space in-between.<ref>{{cite thesis |type=PhD |last=Summar |first=Sarah Page |date=December 2012 |title=Fidget, Sway, and Swerve: Three Works Inspired by Movement from the Intricate Maneuvers Series |publisher=University of North Texas |url=https://digital.library.unt.edu/ark%3A/67531/metadc177259/m2/1/high_res_d/dissertation.pdf}}</ref>
== National Married Couple Rocks Summit == The '''National Married Couple Rocks Summit Liaison Council''' has been formed by 10 tourist spots in Japan that have married couple rocks or rocks for married couples, and is holding the National Married Couple Rocks Summit.
